description: TaterTech is a team of physics graduates and students combining physical modeling with data science to tackle climate adaptation in agriculture.
summary:
Deciding what to plant next season is usually habit and local memory, not the data that's actually shifting the field: changing rainfall, warming seasons, soil quietly depleted by last crops. Most farmers can't easily check that, because real ground-truth data (soil moisture, local temperature trends) either doesn't exist for their field or costs more than a smallholder operation can justify. Satellite-derived products close that gap: Public NASA POWER and the Earth-observation-scale data behind it mean almost any point on the planet already has a usable weather and soil-moisture record, no in-field sensor required.

Our crop rotation recommendation tool uses that directly. Given a farm's location, it confirms a crop can actually survive there before recommending it, runs the same FAO-56 water-demand method used for real irrigation planning, and ranks 3-year rotations by soil health, water, resilience and revenue.

We tell it as a story, not a spreadsheet: watch your current rotation lose to soil depletion, then watch the recommended one win the rematch, same real numbers underneath. Crop rotation is one of the cheapest tools a farmer has, and almost nobody's checking real satellite data before suggesting one. We are.
details:
When starting this project, our main focus was to find a creative and engaging way to present crop rotation recommendations. Our first goal was to transform complex environmental and agricultural information into clear visual elements, such as images, interactive maps and crop cards, allowing users to easily understand and compare different planting strategies.

This is where the idea of a ‘game’ started to form and an initial design of the interactive user interface was planned. During the planning stage, we explored a variety of concepts, including a plant tracker that displays the current growth stage of a crop, an interactive map that allows users to select locations visually rather than entering coordinates, and a Pokémon-inspired system where users can ‘battle’ against different types of environmental challenges such as droughts and floods.

With these ideas in mind, our goal was not simply to present data, but to help users act on it. By combining NASA Earth observation data with crop recommendations, we hoped to help users compare options, understand trade-offs, and make more sustainable farming decisions. Through the creative design, we hoped to engage a wider audience making complex scientific information more accessible, engaging and intuitive.

What it does / how it works

Our crop rotation recommendation tool takes a farm's location and what the farmer actually cares about (soil health, water, drought resilience, revenue) and pulls live NASA POWER weather data and global SoilGrids soil data for that exact point, not a regional average. Before any crop is scored, it checks whether that crop can actually survive the site's real temperature pattern across a full year of data, so something that can't grow there is dropped before it's ever ranked, rather than silently recommended. For every crop that passes, it computes real seasonal water demand using the FAO-56 Penman-Monteith method (the same method used for real irrigation planning), scores 3-year rotation candidates on soil health, water availability, drought resilience and revenue, and ranks them two independent ways: a standard weighted-sum method (SAW) and TOPSIS, reporting whether the two agree. Every ranked rotation comes back with a plain-language explanation and a stated list of what the model doesn't know, not just a number.

Like the members of TaterTech, our algorithm combines the scientific method with data science. Using a composite rotational suitability index (RSI) for different candidate three year sequences, we calculate the suitability of each option. The RSI is calculated as follows:

We calculate the weights and scores for each priority, soil health, water, resilience and revenue. Where the w terms represent the farmer’s priority weights, adjusting them such that the sum of the weights equals 1. The s terms show the given score for each priority, these scores are determined each year and hold a score between 0 and 1. For the soil score we consider factors of nitrogen level, carbon level, root depth and erosion. Both the soil moisture and rainfall contribute to the water score, such that the crop’s water demand is easier to reach if the soil moisture is already high. We use a direct look up to the crop’s drought tolerance to determine the resilience score. The revenue score is determined by yield only. The 'prefactor' 0.9^(t-1) ensures that the near term has a greater impact on the RSI.

Benefits

A farmer, extension worker or NGO gets ranked rotation options for a specific point on the planet, backed by live weather and soil data instead of a static regional lookup table. Every result also says what it doesn't know (soil data flagged as estimated where SoilGrids has no reading, erosion protection labeled qualitative not a measured soil-loss model, revenue labeled yield-only not a real profit figure), so nobody downstream mistakes a design choice for a measured fact. That honesty is treated as a feature, not a disclaimer buried in fine print.

Beyond optimal crop rotations, our model delivers further benefits. Pest control is a huge issue for many farmers, with huge numbers of crops being lost each year. While we don't directly target pest issues, we prevent pest build up by ensuring that the same plant family is not planted twice within two years. In addition, sustainability is an issue that is increasing in importance. To address this we linked our model to the Sustainable Development Goals (SDG) by the United Nations, such that crop rotations that reflect any of the SDGs are awarded a badge.

Intended impact

Rotation is one of the cheapest, highest-leverage changes a farmer can make for soil health and water use, but choosing well needs local climate and soil data most farmers can't easily get. By making the "can this crop even grow here" check and the real water-demand math queryable from just a location, this lowers the barrier to a genuinely climate-informed rotation decision almost anywhere NASA POWER has coverage, which is nearly the whole planet.

Tools, languages, hardware, software

Python backend: FastAPI, pandas, numpy, pydantic. 61 automated tests (pytest), including a check against FAO-56's own published worked example, not just internal consistency checks. Data from the NASA POWER Daily Point API and ISRIC SoilGrids v2.0. No GPU or special hardware required; runs on a laptop, same as the deployed API. Claude Code was used as a development assistant throughout (full disclosure of where and how is in AI_USAGE.md in our repo).

Creativity

Two things we think are genuinely unusual here. First, a bare-field-days metric: a simple, honestly-caveated estimate of how many days a year a given crop leaves soil without living cover, which turns the brief's own "highlight when fields are typically bare" prompt into an actual computed number, not just a sentence. Second, we present the recommendation as a short playable sequence rather than a static report: watch a farmer's current rotation struggle against soil depletion, then see the recommended rotation perform differently, same real numbers underneath, built specifically so "why does rotation order matter" is something you see happen rather than read a paragraph about.

When choosing how to present our website, we chose to base it off Pokemon games. Our game-inspired friendly interface offered an accessible and fun experience for a wide age range of users. Furthermore, the interactive map and sliders would motivate users to test different crop rotations and provide them with a better understanding of the long-term impacts of farming decisions. Using a ‘game’ format supplied a visual representation of crop traits and the matching Pokemon styled cards deepened comprehension of important factors such as soil PH, ideal temperatures and growing time. 

Factors our team considered

We were explicit, throughout, about what's literature-backed versus our own construction, and said so in the project itself rather than only in a README. We stress-tested the pipeline against three very different real climates (humid continental, subarctic, tropical), not just our one demo site, and that cross-checking caught two real scoring bugs before anyone outside the team saw them. We considered the real resolution and latency limits of satellite-derived data (NASA POWER's ~55km grid, a 3-5 day reporting lag) and designed defaults around them rather than ignoring them. And we weighed which additional NASA products (SMAP, ECOSTRESS, GEDI) would genuinely strengthen the model against the realistic integration cost in the time we had, and chose to document that tradeoff honestly rather than bolt on an untested data source for its own sake.
